description: Programs are plain expressions, fully inferred without a single type annotation.

intro.text: Reading a program: every line binds a name (name = expression), and the last line is the program's result. There are no keywords, no statements and no return - a program is one big expression, evaluated once.

description: Records are structural: shapes emerge from use, never from a declaration, and field order never matters.

intro.text: You never declare a shape. Using it creates it. The type of { name: "Ada", age: 22 } IS the set of its fields; two records with the same fields have the same type, whatever they are called.

intro.code:
record Person(string Name, int Age);
var p = new Person("Ada", 22);
intro.caption: For comparison, nominal typing (C#) needs the declaration before the value:

intro.text: TypeFighter goes the other way round: pass ANY record carrying a name field to a function that reads r.name and it type-checks. The declaration does not exist.

name: Functions

examples.title: identity
higher-order
compose
partial application
method-call chaining (UFCS)

description: Functions are curried and first class: partial application, higher-order composition and full polymorphism, all inferred.

intro.text: Every function takes exactly ONE argument; multi-parameter functions are nested lambdas (currying), and f(a, b) is sugar for f(a)(b), so passing fewer arguments is not an error but partial application.

Any function is also a method (UFCS, Uniform Function Call Syntax): x.f(args) is uniformly rewritten to f(x, args), no classes or extension declarations involved, and chains compose left to right. Any expression works as a receiver, including function parameters, so chains are abstractable.

Resolution is by scope, not by type or shape: if f is a visible function (user binding, prelude, namespace member), x.f(args) applies that function; otherwise f is the record-field accessor. Conceptually a record field IS a function, namely the accessor of type { f: a & ... } -> a, so the dot always means 'apply f to x', and a visible function simply shadows the implicit accessor.

Edge cases of the scope rule: (1) a record field named like a visible function is unreachable via CALL syntax. That is ordinary shadowing; read it without call parens instead (g = r.f, then g(x)). (2) Plain x.f without parens always stays a field access.

description: Arrays are homogeneous (Array<T>). Indexing, head and length are ordinary polymorphic functions. xs[i] is just sugar for at(xs)(i).

intro.text: Indexing is not a special form: xs[i] is ordinary sugar for at(xs)(i), and head/length are plain polymorphic functions from the prelude.

description: Operators desugar to prelude calls (op_add, op_lt, and so on). Plus and the comparisons are constrained-polymorphic over Number | String. The logical operators are Boolean-only, equality is fully polymorphic.

intro.text: Operators are prelude functions in disguise: + is op_add. Plus and the comparisons are constrained-polymorphic, their type variable ranges over the SET {Number, String}. One operator, several types, still fully checked per use site.

name: Step protocol (monadic)
description: A record carrying the reserved field __machine is a step machine. Binding one with = is a monadic bind: the name becomes the per-step value. Streams are one interpretation of the protocol; the emit compiles a whole block into a single flat C# state machine.

examples.title: useMemo: lazy constant
let-chain = bind
compose: step values + pure functions
user-defined step fn
custom step record (no useMemo)
branching: cap a counter at 4

intro.text: A record carrying the field __machine is a step machine: inside it, init is the starting state and step maps a state to a value plus the next state. That is the entire protocol - structural, nothing declared, nothing registered, no classes and no interfaces. __machine is the only reserved field name in the language; init, step, val and nextState are ordinary names, read as protocol fields only in this position, so they can never collide with your own records.

intro.code: useMemo = a => { __machine: { init: a, step: s => { val: s, nextState: s } } }
intro.caption: useMemo, the smallest stdlib block, complete implementation:

intro.text: Binding a step value is a monadic bind: in i = count, the name i is the per-step value (a Number), not the machine itself. The solver lifts the binding, and the emit weaves every step of a block into a single flat C# state machine; plain values act as return. Time-driven streams are one interpretation of the protocol - async or other step-by-step effects could reuse the same mechanics.

Known soft spots (the pre-solve desugar decides structurally): a stream produced by your own function call used in argument position, and a plain value passed to your own stream-taking function, currently type-check but fail at runtime, so prefer prelude blocks for those shapes for now. Partial application of stream functions is rejected by the type checker.

name: Streams (time-driven)
description: The host interprets the step protocol over TIME: one step per sample instant. In the playground that is a 10-tick preview, in a computed curve it is the real sample times. count and now are the built-in time-driven streams.

examples.title: count: tick counter
now: sample time

intro.text: The host decides what a step means. The playground preview runs 10 ticks; a computed curve steps once per sample instant. count numbers the steps and now is the sample time in seconds; everything else is derived arithmetic over them.

description: Stream blocks imported from the DSP library, organised in namespaces (math, gen, logic, dsp). The source is always the FIRST argument, and method-call syntax works on any block.

intro.text: 51 blocks imported from the DSP stream library, purely BY TYPE: the language only knows their signatures, the implementations stay in the library. Namespaces (math, gen, logic, dsp) are ordinary record bindings. The source is always the FIRST argument, which is exactly why method-call syntax and chains read naturally.
